name: dashu (dashu-int)
baseline: GMP (mpz via the rug 1.30.0 crate, GMP 6.x)
workload: Criterion microbenchmarks of unsigned big-integer add/sub/mul/div/gcd/pow/modular ops swept over 10 to 10^4 bits, plus small-value (<=128 bit) workloads and string round-trips, dashu-int 0.4.2 vs rug (GMP), ibig, num-bigint and malachite.
claimed_speedup: Third-party report: dashu faster than rug (GMP) in 123 of 205 head-to-head cases and in 98 of 153 small-value cases; ubig_add at 100 bits 3.7 ns vs 21.9 ns, ubig_add_by_class one_word ~3.3 ns vs ~21 ns (typically 2-6x faster on tiny values). GMP wins from ~1000 bits up, e.g. ubig_mul at 10^4 bits rug ~4.5 us vs dashu ~12.8 us.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.92.0 (2025-12-08); cargo bench (default bench/release profile implied, no explicit flags stated); criterion 1 s warm-up, 2 s measurement, 100 samples; rug 1.30.0 linked to GMP 6.x
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no_std, inline storage for values up to two words, so no heap allocation for small integers. Slower than GMP from about 1000 bits upward (GMP has tuned assembly and asymptotically faster algorithms). Rust API, so usable from C++ only through FFI. Not an mpz-compatible API.
caveats: The benchmark code and report live in a separate third-party repo (DRMacIver/rust-bigint-benchmarks, originally written for but not merged into dashu) whose own report calls the numbers 'quick, machine-specific local numbers, not authoritative'. Single laptop (Apple M2 Max), short measurement time, bit-width sweep capped at 10^4 bits, so the large-operand regime where GMP dominates is not covered. Compiler flags are the cargo bench default (optimized bench profile) and are not spelled out in the report, so tier A is borderline; drop to C if an explicit flag listing is required. The dashu README itself makes no GMP speed claim. Another benchmark (tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs, 71 stars, large-number e/fib tasks) shows rug/GMP fastest overall and dashu slower.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'big integer library faster than GMP benchmark github' surfaced DRMacIver/rust-bigint-benchmarks benchmark-report.md

name: blip_mp
baseline: GMP 6.3.0 (mpz_t; built with assembly and with --disable-assembly)
workload: Own bench executable (blip_mp_bench) timing add/sub/mul/divMod/powm/invMod on pre-built pools of values at sizes from i64-range up to 98304 bits, e.g. 5M iterations of r = pool[i % 256] + pool[(i+1) % 256], against mpz_* in a C program using the same libc malloc.
claimed_speedup: On Apple Silicon: all i64-fitting values 1.95-2.66x faster than GMP; RSA 1024/2048/3072-bit mul 1.19-1.45x; RSA-2048 mul 1.16x, divMod 1.31x, powm 1.11x (README also says 13% faster powm at RSA-2048, 21% at 1024-bit); add at 768 bits and up 1.04-1.28x; sub at 256 bits and up 1.03-2.11x; 2048/1024-bit long division 24% faster. Loses to GMP-with-asm on x86_64 (GMP asm is 1.65-3.88x faster than GMP-noasm on Zen 4) and on 128-bit add/sub, 16384+ bit multiply (0.55-0.87x) and modular inverse (2.5-4x behind).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0 ReleaseFast for blip_mp; GMP 6.3.0 from nixpkgs compiled with clang -O3; libc malloc for both; built with `nix build .#bench`
hardware: Apple M4 (aarch64-darwin, macOS 26.x) headline; cross-check on AMD Ryzen 9 7940HS (Zen 4, ~5.0 GHz boost) under NixOS
tradeoffs: Variable-length self-describing byte storage with small-buffer optimization instead of limb arrays; pure Zig, no inline assembly, C FFI exists. Integers only (no mpf/mpq/mpfr). FFT multiplication is implemented but disabled because Toom-3 still wins in the supported range, so it falls behind GMP past ~16K bits. Win is specific to Apple Silicon: on x86_64 GMP's hand-written assembly beats it by 1.5-4x on large operands.
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo (LICENSE, LICENSE-MIT and LICENSE-APACHE all 404 on raw); README says 'MIT or Apache-2.0 (TBD before tagging a release)', so license is treated as unclear and usability is reference. Research-grade; numbers are single-run or 3-run hand medians on one machine, with no statistical sampling, and the bench is the author's own. The author reports the GMP asm advantage on aarch64 is about 0% on M-series, so the win partly reflects GMP's weaker arm64 tuning. Very new repo (BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md has a run dated 2026-04-30, nearly all commits are from May 2026), 1 star.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github multiprecision integer library AVX-512 IFMA faster than GMP mpz_mul benchmark' surfaced pmarreck/blip_mp

name: Swift-BigInt (BInt)
baseline: GMP (README compares against mini-gmp and 'GMP'; plain GMP is described as not counted because it is not portable)
workload: README benchmark of fib(100,000) with big-integer addition and multiplication, plus successive factorials with printing, BInt vs GMP/mini-gmp (Benchmarks.swift).
claimed_speedup: 'BInt about twice as fast as mini-gmp'; 'BInt can add numbers about 2 times faster than GMP (272ms vs 530ms for fib(100,000)), and multiplication is more than twice as fast'; 'when calculating and printing factorials successively, BInt performs significantly better than GMP'.
tradeoffs: Swift-only arbitrary-precision integers and fractions (BInt, BDouble) with an operator-based API; unusable from C++ without a bridge. No assembly, portable.
caveats: First-party README claim without hardware, compiler flags or dataset, and the README text is ambiguous about whether the baseline is mini-gmp (the portable GMP subset without assembly kernels) or full GMP. The README says the benchmarks run more than 10x faster in release than debug mode, so build configuration matters and is unstated. A 2x win over GMP on large-ish Fibonacci addition is surprising for GMP's assembly; treat as unverified.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'big integer library faster than GMP benchmark github' surfaced mkrd/Swift-BigInt README section 'About performance'

name: CGBN (Cooperative Groups Big Numbers)
baseline: GMP 6.1.2 with OpenMP on a 20-core Xeon E5-2698v4
workload: Batched fixed-size unsigned multiple-precision operations (128 to 8192 bits): add, sub, low mul, Montgomery reduce, powm_odd, div_qr, sqrt, gcd, mod inverse; Tesla V100 CGBN kernels vs GMP running on all 20 CPU cores via OpenMP, generated by the bundled perf_tests tools.
claimed_speedup: Average speed-up over GMP+OpenMP: add 77.4x, sub 77.1x, mul (low) 43.5x, mont_reduce 29.3x, powm_odd 21.4x, div_qr 14.4x, sqrt 11.3x, gcd 6.9x, mod inv 4.1x (add at 128 bits 174.3x; powm_odd 16.8-24.6x across 128-8192 bits).
hardware: NVIDIA Tesla V100 (Volta) GPU vs Intel Xeon E5-2698v4 20-core at 2.2 GHz, GMP 6.1.2 with OpenMP
tradeoffs: Header-only C++/CUDA library for fixed-size (32 to 32K bits, multiple of 32) unsigned integers, 4/8/16/32 threads per number; needs batches of independent operations to saturate the GPU; a cgbn_env_t is fixed at one size. Needs CUDA 10+; GMP and Google Test needed only for tests and benchmarks.
caveats: GPU-versus-CPU comparison, not like-for-like hardware (one V100 vs a 20-core 2.2 GHz Xeon). README gives hardware and GMP version but no compiler flags (they are in the makefile), and the numbers date from the Oct 2018 XMP 2.0 beta; the repo's latest commit is a typo fix. Speedups shrink with operand size and for gcd/mod inverse (README itself lists GCD as not optimal). Throughput of many small operations, not latency of one big one.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github GPU big integer multiplication library speedup over GMP CUDA benchmark repository' led to NVlabs/CGBN README

name: MultiFloats.jl
workload: Extended-precision (128-256 bit, 30-60 digit) floating-point arithmetic, e.g. +, -, *, / and linear algebra such as 400x400 QR, versus Julia BigFloat (MPFR), Quadmath.jl and DoubleFloats.jl.
claimed_speedup: README: 'At 30-digit precision, MultiFloats.jl is 30x faster than BigFloat, 6x faster than Quadmath.jl, and 2x faster than DoubleFloats.jl.'
tradeoffs: Fixed small number of Float64 limbs (Float64x2/x3/x4, Float32x2-4), so precision is limited to roughly 106-212 bits rather than arbitrary; no dynamic allocation, branch-free algorithms usable on CPU and GPU in Julia. Transcendental functions fall back to MPFR. Julia only, so C++ use means a port.
caveats: The README numbers have no stated hardware, Julia version or dataset; the benchmark gist (3e10463843f4ab5f5a4a2206c877771b) contains code but no results. The README links an SC'25 paper on the branch-free algorithms; search-result text said it reports up to 35.6x over MPFR and 41.4x over FLINT, but that page was blocked in this session and was not opened, so the tier is not raised to B. Baseline is MPFR only indirectly (Julia BigFloat wraps MPFR); the speedup is for a limited-precision regime where MPFR pays allocation overhead.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'MultiFloats.jl faster than BigFloat MPFR benchmark'

name: DoubleFloats.jl
workload: BenchmarkTools timings on vectors of 1000 values and 50x50 matrices for dot, elementwise add and multiply, exp, matrix multiply and determinant, Double64 vs Float128 (libquadmath) and Big128 (BigFloat with setprecision 128).
claimed_speedup: Relative time, Double64 = 1 vs Big128: dot(v,v) 7, v.+v 16, v.*v 25, exp.(m) 6, m*m 9, det(m) 11 (vs Float128: 3, 7, 12, 2, 3, 5).
tradeoffs: Double-double arithmetic: about 85-106 accurate bits with the Float64 exponent range, not arbitrary precision. Julia only.
caveats: README says 'these results are from BenchmarkTools, on one machine' with no hardware or Julia version given and no linked benchmark code. Ratios are relative and rounded to integers. The comparison point is BigFloat at 128 bits, the regime where MPFR pays per-operation allocation and where double-double is naturally strong.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'DoubleFloats.jl OR double-double library github faster than BigFloat MPFR benchmark'

name: gnu-mpfr-cgbn (MPFR with CUDA/CGBN backend)
baseline: GNU MPFR 4.2.1 (scalar, one CPU core; GMP 6.3.0)
workload: Batched mpfr_mul, fma, div, sqrt, add at precisions 128 to 65536 bits and batch sizes 1 to 16384, comparing scalar MPFR in a loop on one core with the CGBN GPU backend, either including PCIe transfers (batch) or on device-resident data (resident); bit-identical results.
claimed_speedup: Resident vs one-core MPFR at n=16384: fma 284x at 8192 bits, mul 230.3x at 4096 bits, div 157x at 16384 bits, add 120x at 8192 bits, sqrt 115x at 16384 bits. Batch including transfers, n=1024: div 30.4x and sqrt 28.2x at 32768 bits, mul 21.2x at 49152 bits, fma 18.3x at 40960 bits. Single operations (n=1) and add in batch mode are slower than the CPU; div and sqrt above 32768 bits are slower than the CPU.
compiler_and_flags: NVCCFLAGS -O3 -arch=<native or sm_xx> -Xcompiler -fPIC; CUDA 13.2, driver 595.71.05; host compiler flags not stated
hardware: NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (sm_120, 82 SMs, 31.4 GiB) vs one core of the same machine's CPU (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Optional --enable-cgbn build of MPFR with batch and device-vector interfaces (mpfr_cgbn_*); precision up to 65536 bits on the GPU, above that falls back to CPU. Needs an NVIDIA GPU (compute capability 3.5+) and CUDA toolkit. Only pays off with batches of at least 64-1024 operations; the author recommends 4096-16384 bits with batches of a few thousand.
caveats: GPU-versus-one-CPU-core comparison, so the headline 230x/284x is not a like-for-like speedup against a parallel CPU run; the CPU model is not stated, which keeps the tier at C even though benchmark code (tests/cgbnbench, `gmake bench-cgbn`) is public. Repo was created 2026-09-12 with a single 'Initial Github commit', so there is no history; it is a derived copy of the GNU MPFR 4.2.1 source tree plus the CGBN backend rather than a GitHub fork. The CGBN library itself (NVlabs/CGBN) is a separate project.

name: bigfft
baseline: Go math/big (README also benchmarks GMP, which is faster)
workload: Multiplication of random big integers from 1 kB to 100 MB and decimal-string scanning of 10^3 to 10^7 digits, bigfft Schonhage-Strassen vs Go math/big and vs GMP.
claimed_speedup: vs math/big multiplication: 1 Mb 105237800 ns -> 28446400 ns (-72.97%), 10 Mb -89.43%, 100 Mb 147599836000 -> 5921594000 ns (-95.99%); decimal scan of 1e6 digits 1776707489 -> 144867502 ns (-91.85%). Versus GMP, bigfft is slower at every size (e.g. 1 Mb 12100000 ns GMP vs 22391830 ns bigfft; 100 Mb 2673000000 vs 5228991000 ns).
hardware: Core 2 Quad Q8200 (2.33 GHz) for multiplication; Core i5-4590 for decimal scanning
tradeoffs: Go package using FFT (Schonhage-Strassen) multiplication above about 200 kbits and plugging into math/big types; the README says it is a toy proof of concept that is not expected to be used in production. Go only.
caveats: Does not beat GMP: the README's GMP table shows GMP about 1.2x to 3.1x faster at every size (derived from page data: bigfft ns/op divided by GMP ns/op). The win is over Go's math/big only (baseline_in_list false for the Go baseline). Old CPUs, Go version and flags unstated, and the last commit is January 2023. Included as a documented FFT-multiplication reference rather than a GMP-beater.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'big integer library faster than GMP benchmark github' surfaced remyoudompheng/bigfft

name: APFP (arbitrary precision floating point on FPGA)
baseline: MPFR (the repo's CPU reference implementation uses mpfr_t; the README itself only says '36-core dual-socket Xeon node')
workload: 512-bit arbitrary-precision floating-point matrix-matrix multiplication (MAC throughput) on a Xilinx Alveo U250 FPGA versus a CPU node, per the FCCM'22 paper.
claimed_speedup: README: 'instantiations of the design on an Alveo U250 accelerator were shown to yield 2.0 GMAC/s of 512-bit matrix-matrix multiplication; an order of magnitude higher than a 36-core dual-socket Xeon node, corresponding to 375x CPU cores worth of throughput'.
hardware: Xilinx Alveo U250 FPGA vs 36-core dual-socket Xeon node (CPU model not stated in the README)
tradeoffs: Fully pipelined multiplier and adder (Karatsuba-based) generated with Vitis HLS for XRT-enabled Xilinx FPGAs, exposed as a matrix-multiplication primitive; fixed width chosen at compile time (multiple of 512 bits, 63-bit exponent); needs Vitis, XRT, GMP and MPFR. Useless without the specific FPGA hardware.
caveats: The README does not name MPFR as the CPU baseline; this is inferred from the repo's host/TestMatrixMultiplication.cpp, which checks results against an MPFR reference implementation, and from the paper title. The linked FCCM'22 paper PDF was blocked in this session so its methodology and CPU model could not be read; a paper would make this tier B. No LICENSE file found on raw (404), and the page showed no license. Last commit May 2022.
found_via: GitHub: topic page https://github.com/topics/bignum (spcl/apfp listed as APFP) and WebSearch snippets about FPGA arbitrary precision vs MPFR

name: mp++
baseline: GMP 6.2.0 (mpz_t, benchmarked through Boost.Multiprecision gmp_int calling the GMP API directly)
workload: Vectors of 3x10^7 random small integers (1-limb static size, unsigned and signed, also 2-limb): dot product, element-wise multiply-add, division, GCD, LCM, left shift, conversion and sorting, mp++ integer vs GMP, Boost cpp_int, FLINT fmpzxx and builtin 64/128-bit integers.
claimed_speedup: Docs: 1-limb unsigned dot product 'mp++ is almost 4 times faster than GMP'; vector multiply-add 'more than 7 times faster than GMP'; vector division 'mp++ and FLINT ... are about 8 times faster than GMP'. Slowdown versus builtin 64-bit integers is x4 (dot product), less than x3 (multiply-add).
compiler_and_flags: Per doc/benchmarks.rst: GCC 10.1 with mp++ 0.21, GMP 6.2.0, Boost 1.73.0, FLINT 2.5.2; the benchmark CMake target uses the project's Release flags (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE defaults to Release), exact flag values not quoted in the docs
tradeoffs: C++ library layered on GMP/MPFR/MPC; the win comes from the small-value optimization (values up to a fixed number of limbs live inline, no heap allocation), so it applies to 1-2 limb operands and large operands defer to GMP speed.
caveats: Evidence upgrade for a catalogued project (is_evidence_for_known): the earlier record had no hardware or compiler. Results were last updated 2020-06-09 and the Ryzen 3950x and GCC 10.1 are old; the benchmarks only cover 1-limb and 2-limb integers, the regime where GMP's fixed per-object overhead dominates. Build flags come from the CMake Release default rather than being listed in the docs.
found_via: GitHub: raw doc/benchmarks.rst and doc/integer_benchmarks.rst in bluescarni/mppp, opened while checking the mp++ record

name: uint256 (holiman)
workload: Go benchmarks (go test -bench) of fixed 256-bit unsigned arithmetic: add, sub, mul, square, div, sqrt, shifts, bitwise ops, hex/decimal conversion, uint256 vs big.Int with time/op, B/op and allocs/op.
claimed_speedup: README: 'uint256 wins over math/big in every single case, often with orders of magnitude' (as of 2020-03-18). Examples: Add/single 1.99 ns vs 18.11 ns (-89.02%), Mul/single 12.10 ns vs 57.69 ns (-79.03%), Square/single 12.49 ns vs 56.10 ns (-77.74%), SDiv/large 94.64 ns vs 642.10 ns (-85.26%), FromDecimalString 7973 ns vs 32850 ns (-75.73%), zero allocations.
stars_or_usage: 383 stars; used by go-ethereum and erigon
tradeoffs: Fixed 256-bit width only (not arbitrary precision), alloc-free value type replacing big.Int in Ethereum clients; overflow wraps modulo 2^256.
caveats: Baseline is Go's math/big, not GMP or MPFR, so baseline_in_list is false; included as the incumbent for Go big-integer use. The README gives the benchmark commands (go test -bench) but no CPU model, Go version or date for the table besides 'as of 2020-03-18'. Fixed-width versus arbitrary-width comparison favors the specialised type.
found_via: GitHub: direct check of github.com/holiman/uint256 while surveying Go/Rust fixed-width integer libraries after topic pages (github.com/topics/biginteger)
